newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds push higher, buoyed by U.S. ECI data.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds push higher, buoyed by U.S. ECI data.

text.p: Irish government bonds pushed higher in afternoon trade on Tuesday as international markets moved up following the release of lower-than-expected U.S. employment cost data, dealers said.
The fourth quarter ECI, which measures wages plus benefits, was up by 0.8 percent compared with expectations of a 0.9 percent rise, and helped ease market fears about inflation and a Fed rate rise.
"It's a good result to get a figure like that especially as we've seen Greenspan talk about it," one dealer said. "We feel we can make further progress from here."

The Irish market gained 30-40 pence on the data, shrugging off a rise in U.S. January consumer confidence to 116.8 from a revised 114.2 in December, which saw U.S. Treasuries trim their earlier gains.
Dealers said five-year and 10-year Irish paper attracted good interest in particular and spreads over Germany had narrowed by three to four basis points.

By 1613 GMT, the eight percent 10-year bond was at 109.55 to yield 6.50 percent, up from an earlier low of 108.95 and 45 pence higher on the day. Dealers said it was yielding around 88 basis points over the German equivalent.
"As soon as the spread over Germany widens out to 93 to 95 basis points, we have seen buying interest," a dealer said.
Five-year paper also gained ground, firming nearly 30 pence to 102.73 to yield 5.71 percent.

Looking ahead, traders said the market was keeping a close eye on union voting on Partnership 2000, the new wage agreement between Irish unions, employers and workers. Ireland's largest union, SIPTU, was due to vote on the accord on Tuesday ahead of a full union ballot on Thursday.

Rejection of the agreement, which provides for wage increases totalling 9.25 percent over a three-year period, would take the ceiling off wage increases and would not bode well for Ireland's inflation outlook, analysts said.
"It could augur for higher wage inflation as the current strength of economic conditions favours employees over employers in one-to-one wage negotiations," Riada Stockbrokers said.
"Hence it would tend to bias up the outlook for inflation if employers were to recoup higher wage demands through increases in retail prices," the broker added.
